MCMC diagnostics

Estimated time: 75 minutes

Slides

Introduction

In the previous session, you saw how MCMC algorithms explore posterior distributions by taking random walks through parameter space. You implemented Metropolis-Hastings yourself and used Turing.jl’s NUTS to do the same thing with gradients. What we haven’t addressed: how do you know the sampler actually worked?

MCMC comes with weak guarantees. A chain always returns numbers, but nothing forces those numbers to be representative samples from the posterior. Chains get stuck, wander with no clear trend, or mix so slowly that a thousand “samples” are effectively a dozen. The convergence theorems only kick in as the number of iterations goes to infinity, which is not a length of run anyone actually does. Take unreliable output at face value and you end up with the wrong point estimates and overconfident intervals.

This session covers how to catch those failures before they end up in a paper: trace plots for the visual check, R̂ and effective sample size for the numerical ones, and a few standard failure modes worth keeping in mind.

ImportantWhat convergence means

A chain has converged when the distribution of its draws has reached the posterior and stays there however long you keep sampling. That is a statement about the chain in the limit, so no run of finite length can establish it.

This is why the rest of the session is a set of checks rather than a test. Each diagnostic can tell you that something has gone wrong. None of them can tell you that nothing has. A chain that passes all of them has failed to show a problem.

Objectives

The aim is to learn how to assess whether your MCMC chains have converged and whether your posterior samples are reliable enough to base conclusions on.

In this session, you will:

  1. Diagnose chains visually using trace plots and other visualisations
  2. Run several chains and say what their agreement does and does not show
  3. Calculate quantitative diagnostics like R̂ and effective sample size
  4. Identify common failure modes and how to fix them
  5. Use Turing.jl’s built-in diagnostics for automated checking
  6. Apply best practices for robust MCMC in practice

Setup

Source file

The source file of this session is located at sessions/mcmc_diagnostics.qmd.

Load libraries

using Random ## for random numbers
using Distributions ## for probability distributions
using DifferentialEquations ## for differential equations
using DataFrames ## for data frames
using Plots ## for plots
using StatsPlots ## for statistical plots
using Turing ## for probabilistic programming and MCMC
using FlexiChains ## chain objects and diagnostics
using FlexiChains: niters, nchains ## public, but not exported, so name them
using StatsBase ## for autocorrelation

Initialisation

We set a random seed for reproducibility. Setting this ensures that you should get exactly the same results on your computer as we do.

Random.seed!(12345)
TaskLocalRNG()

Load data and model from previous session

We’ll use the same SIR model and epidemic data from previous sessions.

NoteSIR model definition (from src/sir_model.jl) 
using DifferentialEquations
using Distributions
using DataFrames

"""
    sir_ode!(du, u, p, t)

SIR model ordinary differential equations.

# States
- `u[1]` (S): Susceptible
- `u[2]` (I): Infectious
- `u[3]` (R): Recovered

# Parameters
- `p[1]` (R_0): Basic reproduction number
- `p[2]` (D_inf): Infectious period (days)
"""
function sir_ode!(du, u, p, t)
    S, I, R = u
    R_0, D_inf = p
    N = S + I + R

    β = R_0 / D_inf
    ν = 1 / D_inf

    du[1] = -β * S * I / N          # dS/dt
    du[2] = β * S * I / N - ν * I   # dI/dt
    du[3] = ν * I                   # dR/dt
end

"""
    SIR_BASE_PROBLEM

A template `ODEProblem` for `sir_ode!`, built once when the package loads.
`simulate_sir` calls `remake` on it rather than building a fresh problem on
every call, which matters because a likelihood asks for tens of thousands of
simulations. The placeholder state and parameters are never used: `remake`
replaces `u0`, `p` and `tspan` on every call.
"""
const SIR_BASE_PROBLEM = ODEProblem(sir_ode!, zeros(3), (0.0, 1.0), zeros(2))

"""
    simulate_sir(θ, init_state, times)

Simulate the deterministic SIR model.

# Arguments
- `θ`: Dict with keys :R_0, :D_inf
- `init_state`: Dict with keys :S, :I, :R
- `times`: Time points to return (e.g., 0.0:1.0:30.0)

# Returns
DataFrame with columns: time, S, I, R, Inc (daily incidence)

`Inc` is the flow out of S, so `Inc[i]` counts the infections between
`times[i - 1]` and `times[i]`. No such interval precedes the first time point,
so `Inc[1]` is zero and `times` needs a point before the first observation:
`Inc[i + 1]` is the incidence over the day the i-th observation counts.
"""
function simulate_sir(θ, init_state, times)
    u0 = [init_state[:S], init_state[:I], init_state[:R]]
    prob = remake(
        SIR_BASE_PROBLEM;
        u0 = u0,
        p = [θ[:R_0], θ[:D_inf]],
        tspan = (times[1], times[end]),
    )
    sol = solve(prob, Tsit5(), saveat = times)

    df = DataFrame(
        time = sol.t,
        S = [u[1] for u in sol.u],
        I = [u[2] for u in sol.u],
        R = [u[3] for u in sol.u],
    )

    # Daily incidence: new infections, the flow out of S
    df.Inc = [0.0; -diff(df.S)]

    return df
end
# Initial state and time range
init_state = [999, 1, 0]
t0, tend = (0, 30)

# Epidemic data
epi1 = DataFrame(
    time = 1:1:30,
    obs = [
        1, 3, 4, 11, 19, 38, 67, 112, 183, 210, 237, 182, 178, 154, 95, 68, 51,
        30, 32, 18, 19, 9, 2, 2, 2, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0
    ]
)

sir_prob = ODEProblem(sir_ode!, [999, 1, 0], (0.0, 1.0), [2.5, 5.0])

# Define our SIR model in Turing.jl (same as MCMC session)
@model function sir_model(init_state, times, n_obs)
    # Weakly informative priors
    R_0 ~ truncated(Normal(2.5, 1.5), lower=1.0)
    D_inf ~ truncated(Normal(5.0, 3.0), lower=0.5)

    prob = remake(
        sir_prob, u0 = init_state, p = [R_0, D_inf], tspan = (times[1], times[end])
    )
    sol = solve(prob, saveat = times)

    # Likelihood
    I = sol[2, :]
    # Use max to handle tiny numerical errors from automatic differentiation
    lambdas = [max(I[i], 0.0) for i in 1:n_obs]
    obs ~ arraydist(Poisson.(lambdas))
end

# Create model instance
model = sir_model(init_state, epi1.time, length(epi1.obs)) | (; obs = epi1.obs)

Visual diagnostics

1. Trace plots: The most important diagnostic

Trace plots show parameter values over iterations, which is where the chain has been. A well-mixed chain looks like a “hairy caterpillar” - densely filled with rapid up-and-down fluctuations around a stable mean:

# Good chain: well-mixing NUTS
chain_good = sample(model, NUTS(), 2000)
# chain_good[:R_0] extracts the samples for R_0 from the chain object
# You can use this with any parameter name defined in your @model function
plot(
    chain_good[:R_0], title = "Good Chain: R_0", xlabel = "Iteration",
    ylabel = "R_0", linewidth = 1
)
Plotting code 
# For comparison, let's look at the other parameter too
p1 = plot(
    chain_good[:R_0], title = "R_0 Trace", xlabel = "Iteration",
    ylabel = "R_0", linewidth = 1
)
p2 = plot(
    chain_good[:D_inf], title = "D_inf Trace", xlabel = "Iteration",
    ylabel = "D_inf", linewidth = 1
)

plot(p1, p2, layout = (2, 1), size = (800, 600))

Look for a chain that moves freely around parameter space and shows no obvious trend or drift. The opposites are what you want to avoid: a chain stuck in one region, still climbing or descending after warmup, or exploring only a narrow band.

2. Running averages

Running averages should stabilise if the chain has converged:

function running_mean(x)
    return [mean(x[1:i]) for i in eachindex(x)]
end

R_0_samples = vec(chain_good[:R_0])
p1 = plot(
    running_mean(R_0_samples), title = "Running Mean: R_0",
    xlabel = "Iteration", ylabel = "Running Mean R_0", linewidth = 2
)
hline!(
    p1, [mean(R_0_samples)], color = :red, linestyle = :dash,
    label = "Final mean"
)

D_inf_samples = vec(chain_good[:D_inf])
p2 = plot(
    running_mean(D_inf_samples), title = "Running Mean: D_inf",
    xlabel = "Iteration", ylabel = "Running Mean D_inf", linewidth = 2
)
hline!(
    p2, [mean(D_inf_samples)], color = :red, linestyle = :dash,
    label = "Final mean"
)

plot(p1, p2, layout = (2, 1))

3. Autocorrelation

MCMC samples are correlated whatever the sampler, because each draw starts where the last one ended. In NUTS the trajectory carries the state some distance before the momentum is refreshed and the chain forgets where it started (the puck sliding on). Good chains have autocorrelation that decays quickly:

NoteWhat autocorrelation measures

The autocorrelation at lag kk is the correlation between the chain and itself kk steps later:

ρk=Cov⁡(θt,θt+k)Var⁡(θt)\rho_k = \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(\theta_t,\ \theta_{t+k})}{\operatorname{Var}(\theta_t)}

It is 1 at lag 0 and falls towards 0 as the chain forgets where it was. How fast it falls is key, because the sum of the ρk\rho_k is the integrated autocorrelation time

τ=1+2∑k=1∞ρk\tau = 1 + 2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \rho_k

The 1 is the draw with itself at lag 0, and the 2 is because summing the covariances of every pair of draws counts each later lag in both directions. That sum is what correlation does to the precision of a mean,

Var⁡(θ‾)≈σ2N(1+2∑k≥1ρk)=σ2τN\operatorname{Var}(\bar\theta) \approx \frac{\sigma^2}{N}\Big(1 + 2\sum_{k \ge 1}\rho_k\Big) = \frac{\sigma^2 \tau}{N}

so τ\tau is the factor by which correlation inflates the variance of the mean against independent draws, and roughly how many iterations the chain needs to produce one draw’s worth of new information.

Thinning, keeping only every nn-th draw, is the traditional response to a large τ\tau. It is rarely needed with NUTS, whose draws are already close to independent, but it still matters for random-walk samplers.

function autocorr_plot(chain, param_name; max_lag = 100)
    samples = Array(chain[param_name])  # Convert to plain array
    lags = 0:max_lag
    # autocor from StatsBase expects a vector and returns scalar for each lag
    autocorrs = [autocor(samples, [lag])[1] for lag in lags]

    plot(
        lags, autocorrs, title = "Autocorrelation: $param_name",
        xlabel = "Lag", ylabel = "Autocorrelation", linewidth = 2
    )
    hline!([0], color = :gray, linestyle = :dash, label = "")
    hline!(
        [-0.05, 0.05], color = :red, linestyle = :dash, label = "±5% threshold"
    )
end

p1 = autocorr_plot(chain_good, :R_0)
p2 = autocorr_plot(chain_good, :D_inf)

plot(p1, p2, layout = (2, 1), size = (800, 600))

We can see that autocorrelation drops quickly to near zero and both parameters show good mixing. Read the lag at which the curve first stays inside the dashed band: beyond it, samples that far apart carry almost no shared information. The exact lag varies from run to run, which is why the effective sample size below is the number to quote rather than a lag read off a plot.

TipExercise: Interpret the visual diagnostics

Look back at the trace plots, running mean plots, and autocorrelation plots above.

  1. What would a bad trace plot look like? Sketch or describe what you would see if the chain was stuck or not mixing well.
  2. If the running mean was still trending upward after 2000 iterations, what would that suggest?
  3. If autocorrelation remained high (say > 0.5) even at lag 100, what would that indicate about your effective sample size?
TipSolution

A bad trace plot has visible structure where you want noise. A stuck chain shows long flat stretches, every proposal rejected. A badly mixing one drifts slowly across the space like a random walk rather than crossing it repeatedly. The healthy version looks like a hairy caterpillar: dense, and the same on the left as on the right.

A running mean still trending at 2000 iterations means the chain has not forgotten where it started. Either burn-in was too short, or, more worryingly, the chain is still travelling towards a region it has not reached. Running longer tells you which: a burn-in problem settles, an exploration problem keeps going.

Autocorrelation above 0.5 at lag 100 means successive samples carry almost no new information, so the effective sample size is a small fraction of the number of iterations. Ten thousand samples might be worth a few dozen independent ones. The posterior mean can still be roughly right while the standard error you would report from it is badly optimistic.

4. Several chains

Every diagnostic so far has looked at a single chain. A trace plot tells you that the chain moves freely around the region it is in. It cannot tell you whether that region is the whole posterior, because the chain has never been anywhere else. A chain that settles into one part of the posterior and explores that part thoroughly looks healthy on all three plots above.

Running several chains is what makes that failure visible. Each chain is initialised separately, so they start in different places. If chains that started apart end up describing the same distribution, that is evidence they have found the posterior. If they end up describing different distributions, at least one of them is wrong. Four chains is often used as a default, and the code below asks for at most four and at least two, so it adapts to the threads your machine has.

NoteRunning Julia with multiple threads

To run multiple chains in parallel, Julia must be started with multiple threads. Check your current thread count with Threads.nthreads(). If it shows 1, restart Julia with:

julia -t auto          # Use all available CPU cores
julia -t 4             # Use exactly 4 threads

In VS Code, you can set this permanently in settings: search for “Julia: Num Threads” and set it to “auto” or a specific number. Without multiple threads, chains will run sequentially (slower but still correct).

# Detect available threads to avoid overwhelming CI systems
n_chains = max(2, min(4, Threads.nthreads()))
println("Running $n_chains chains in parallel ($(Threads.nthreads()) threads available)")
chain_multi = sample(model, NUTS(), MCMCThreads(), 2000, n_chains)
TipCode explainer
  • MCMCThreads() - tells Turing to run multiple chains in parallel using Julia threads. Much faster than running sequentially on multi-core machines.
  • sample(model, sampler, MCMCThreads(), n_samples, n_chains) - the extended signature for parallel sampling. Here we request n_chains chains, each with n_samples samples.
  • Threads.nthreads() - returns how many threads Julia has available. Start Julia with julia -t auto to use all CPU cores.

To see what the other outcome looks like, we sample the same model with a deliberately bad sampler. It is Metropolis-Hastings with a random-walk proposal of standard deviation 0.001, far too small to cross the posterior in the iterations it is given.

# 1e-6 chosen after trying 1e-4, which converges within the run
chain_stuck = sample(model, MH([1e-6 0.0; 0.0 1e-6]), MCMCThreads(), 2000, n_chains)
Plotting code 
function chains_trace_plot(chains, param, plot_title)
    p = plot(title = plot_title, xlabel = "Iteration", ylabel = string(param))
    for i in 1:nchains(chains)
        plot!(p, vec(chains[chain = i][param]), linewidth = 1, label = "Chain $i")
    end
    return p
end

p1 = chains_trace_plot(chain_multi, :R_0, "Converged: NUTS")
p2 = chains_trace_plot(chain_stuck, :R_0, "Not converged: random walk with tiny steps")

plot(p1, p2, layout = (2, 1), size = (800, 600))

In the top panel the chains lie on top of each other and you cannot tell them apart. In the bottom panel the chains sit at different levels and are still moving after 2000 iterations. A single chain cannot tell you whether a slow drift is poor mixing or a chain that has not arrived yet, and four chains can.

5. Burn-in and warmup

MCMC chains often start from arbitrary initial values and need time to find the high-probability regions of the posterior. Samples from this initial exploration phase, called burn-in, are discarded because they do not represent the target distribution.

Modern samplers like NUTS have automatic warmup periods where they adapt the step size to achieve good acceptance rates, learn the geometry of the posterior and explore to find typical parameter values.

In our earlier example, when we ran sample(model, NUTS(), 2000), Turing actually ran about 3000 iterations in total: 1000 warmup iterations, automatically discarded, plus 2000 sampling iterations. The returned chain contains only the 2000 post-warmup samples.

By default, NUTS adapts for min(1000, N ÷ 2) iterations, where N is the number of samples you ask for. Asking for 2000 samples therefore gives the 1000 warmup iterations above, while asking for 500 gives 250. The number of warmup iterations is the first argument to NUTS, so NUTS(2000, 0.65) adapts for 2000 iterations at a target acceptance rate of 0.65. For most models the default is sufficient.

With NUTS, you typically do not need to manually discard burn-in samples. The warmup is automatic and adaptive. You should still check the trace plots: a chain still trending after warmup needs longer adaptation.

The default is deliberately conservative, and in practice a shorter warmup is often safe, which is worth having when a model is expensive or refit many times. Treat that as an optimisation to confirm rather than assume. Shorten the adaptation, then check that the trace plots and R̂ are no worse than they were with the default, and that no divergences have appeared.

Quantitative diagnostics

1. R̂ statistic (Gelman-Rubin diagnostic)

R̂ turns that comparison between chains into a number. It weighs the variance within each chain against the variance between chains, and comes out at 1 when the two agree. Vehtari et al. (2021) recommend treating anything above 1.01 as a warning. The older and looser threshold of 1.1 is still widely quoted, and a chain that fails that one is in trouble.

NoteWhere R̂ comes from

Take mm chains of nn iterations each. Write WW for the mean of the within-chain variances, and BB for nn times the variance of the mm chain means.

V̂=n−1nW+1nB\hat{V} = \frac{n - 1}{n} W + \frac{1}{n} B

Both fractions are conversions rather than weights. Each chain’s variance divides that chain’s scatter by n−1n - 1, so multiplying by (n−1)/n(n-1)/n re-expresses the same scatter per draw. BB is nn times the variance of the chain means, so B/nB/n is that variance itself. V̂\hat{V} is therefore the within-chain scatter per draw plus the full spread of the chain means.

Adding that spread in full is what makes V̂\hat{V} an overestimate of the posterior variance while the chains disagree, and WW, which never looks between chains, is an underestimate for as long as any chain is confined to part of the posterior. R̂ compares the two:

R̂=V̂W\hat{R} = \sqrt{\frac{\hat{V}}{W}}

The ratio is against WW because that is the optimistic estimate set against the pessimistic one. The square root puts the answer on the scale of a standard deviation rather than a variance, so 1.01 is a 1% discrepancy in spread.

Chains that have settled in different parts of the posterior disagree about the mean. That inflates BB, and R̂ goes up with it.

Chains that agree do not bring R̂ to exactly 1, though, because the draws within each chain are correlated. The mean of a correlated chain of length nn has variance of about Wτ/nW\tau/n, with τ\tau the integrated autocorrelation time from the autocorrelation callout, and BB is nn times that variance, so BB comes out at roughly τW\tau W. Substituting gives

R̂2=n−1n+BnW≈1+τ−1n\hat{R}^2 = \frac{n - 1}{n} + \frac{B}{nW} \approx 1 + \frac{\tau - 1}{n}

Independent draws are the special case τ=1\tau = 1, where B≈WB \approx W.

The statistic is due to Gelman and Rubin (1992). What rhat() reports is a modified version of it, so a number computed by hand from the formula above will not match what Turing prints; What rhat actually computes in the advanced section says what the modifications are.

# Check what each individual chain found
println("Individual chain summaries:")
for i in 1:n_chains
    chain_i = chain_multi[chain = i]
    r0_mean = mean(chain_i[:R_0])
    dinf_mean = mean(chain_i[:D_inf])
    println(
        "  Chain $i: R_0 = $(round(r0_mean, digits = 2)), ",
        "D_inf = $(round(dinf_mean, digits = 2))"
    )
end

# Calculate R̂, for the converged chains and for the stuck ones
function print_rhat(chains, label)
    println("\nR̂ values, $label:")
    for row in eachrow(DataFrame(rhat(chains)))
        status = row.stat < 1.01 ? "good" : "bad"
        println("  $(row.param): $(round(row.stat, digits = 3)) $status")
    end
end

print_rhat(chain_multi, "NUTS")
print_rhat(chain_stuck, "random walk with tiny steps")
Individual chain summaries:
  Chain 1: R_0 = 2.45, D_inf = 1.95
  Chain 2: R_0 = 2.45, D_inf = 1.95

R̂ values, NUTS:
  R_0: 1.0 good
  D_inf: 1.0 good

R̂ values, random walk with tiny steps:
  R_0: 2.123 bad
  D_inf: 2.123 bad

The second set is the pair of panels from Several chains turned into a number.

TipCode explainer
  • chain_multi[chain = i] - extracts the i-th chain from a multi-chain object. A chain is indexed by iteration and by chain, and niters and nchains give the two sizes.
  • rhat(chain) - calculates the R̂ (Gelman-Rubin) diagnostic. Compares variance within chains to variance between chains. Values below 1.01 mean the chains have not been caught disagreeing; 1.1 is the older, looser threshold.
# Visualise multiple chains
plot(chain_multi)

This adds what the earlier figure did not: the marginal density beside each trace, and both parameters rather than one.

2. Effective sample size (ESS)

ESS tells you how many independent samples your correlated MCMC samples are equivalent to. It is the autocorrelation function from the autocorrelation section read as a single number. The estimator sums the same ρk\rho_k that the plot showed, so the faster that curve decayed the more each draw is worth.

NoteWhere ESS comes from

Using the ρk\rho_k above, from NN draws,

Neff=N1+2∑k=1KρkN_{\text{eff}} = \frac{N}{1 + 2\sum_{k=1}^{K} \rho_k}

The denominator is τ\tau, the integrated autocorrelation time defined in the autocorrelation callout. A chain whose autocorrelations die away quickly has τ\tau near 1 and loses almost nothing. A chain with ρk\rho_k still large at long lags has a large τ\tau and an ESS far below NN.

The sum runs to KK rather than to infinity, and where it is cut matters. Estimated autocorrelations at long lags are mostly noise, and adding more of them makes τ\tau steadily worse rather than steadily better. Geyer (1992) is where the rule for cutting comes from. Turing uses the rank-normalised, across-chain version of Vehtari et al. (2021).

ess_values = DataFrame(ess(chain_multi))
# ESS pools every draw from every chain, so compare it against iterations times chains.
n_samples = niters(chain_multi) * nchains(chain_multi)
4000
TipCode explainer
  • ess(chain) - calculates Effective Sample Size. MCMC samples are correlated, so N samples don’t give you N independent draws. ESS estimates how many independent samples your chain is equivalent to.
println("Effective Sample Size:")
for row in eachrow(ess_values)
    param = row.param
    value = row.stat
    efficiency = value / n_samples * 100
    status = value > 100 ? "good" : "bad"  # Rule of thumb: ESS > 100
    println(
        "  $param: $(round(value, digits = 0)) / $n_samples ",
        "($(round(efficiency, digits = 1))%) $status"
    )
end
Effective Sample Size:
  R_0: 941.0 / 4000 (23.5%) good
  D_inf: 976.0 / 4000 (24.4%) good

An ESS close to N means little autocorrelation and efficient sampling. An ESS much smaller than N means the samples are highly correlated and you need to run longer. As a rule of thumb, ESS below 100 is generally not enough for reliable inference.

ESS can come out slightly above N. NUTS sometimes produces mildly anti-correlated draws, which carry a little more information than independent ones.

The number above is the bulk ESS, which is what ess reports by default.

3. Monte Carlo standard error (MCSE)

When reporting posteriors it is important to understand how accurate the estimates are. MCSE is a way of asking how many digits of a reported number are real, and how many would change with a different seed.

NoteWhere MCSE comes from

For a posterior mean,

MCSE≈posterior SDNeff\text{MCSE} \approx \frac{\text{posterior SD}}{\sqrt{N_{\text{eff}}}}

The posterior SD is the spread you are trying to report. That spread is fixed by the posterior, so ESS is the only lever, and you raise it by sampling longer or by mixing better.

The ESS here is the one for the mean on the untransformed draws, not the bulk ESS printed above, so the two will not reconcile by hand.

mcse_values = DataFrame(mcse(chain_multi))
posterior_means = DataFrame(mean(chain_multi))

println("Posterior means ± MCSE:")
for row in eachrow(mcse_values)
    param = row.param
    mcse_val = row.stat
    mean_val = posterior_means[posterior_means.param .== Ref(param), :stat][1]
    rel_error = mcse_val / abs(mean_val) * 100
    println(
        "  $param: $(round(mean_val, digits = 3)) ± ",
        "$(round(mcse_val, digits = 4)) ",
        "($(round(rel_error, digits = 2))% relative error)"
    )
end
Posterior means ± MCSE:
  R_0: 2.448 ± 0.0012 (0.05% relative error)
  D_inf: 1.947 ± 0.0012 (0.06% relative error)

Report R0=2.31R_0 = 2.31 with an MCSE of 0.05 and the second decimal place is sampler noise, because a different seed moves it. Sample until the MCSE is small next to the precision you want to claim.

Common problems and solutions

Problem 1: Poor mixing (chain gets stuck)

Chains get stuck for a few common reasons: a sampler too basic for the geometry, proposal steps that are the wrong size, or correlated parameters and narrow ridges in the posterior. Multimodality does it too (see Problem 4).

The first two of those are sampler problems and the third is a model problem, and which you are looking at depends on what you are sampling with. On basic Metropolis-Hastings, moving to NUTS is usually the fix, and running longer helps. On NUTS, poor mixing usually means the model, so reparametrise to give the posterior a friendlier shape. Against the chains you are already running, a stuck one shows up as an outlier.

With gradient-based samplers like NUTS, mixing problems are uncommon when the model is specified correctly, the posterior is reasonably well-behaved, and the priors are not pathological.

A chain started where the model cannot be evaluated, or where it raises inference errors, does not move at all, and its trace shows the long flat stretches of a stuck chain. Those look exactly like a badly tuned proposal, which is why this failure is usually misdiagnosed. The flat Uniform(1, 20) prior in the introduction session is the usual way to end up there, and the guards against it are in the Julia ecosystem session and Model checking.

Problem 2: Where the chain starts

Where a chain starts is a choice, and the default does not make it with the prior in mind. For Hamiltonian samplers Turing uses InitFromUniform(), which draws on [−2,2][-2, 2] on the unconstrained scale, following Stan. Under this session’s prior that puts R0R_0 between 1.1 and 8.4, but under Uniform(1, 20) it puts R0R_0 between 3.3 and 17.7, so no chain can start near the 2.4 the posterior settles on. InitFromPrior() and InitFromParams((; R_0 = 2.5, D_inf = 2.0)) are the alternatives, passed through initial_params. Drawing from the prior is only as good as the prior, though: Uniform(1, 20) puts R0R_0 above 15 about a quarter of the time, which is what the default does too.

Problem 3: Divergent transitions (for HMC/NUTS)

NUTS simulates a puck sliding over the posterior surface. A divergent transition occurs when the simulation becomes numerically unstable — the puck “flies off” to implausible values instead of following the contour. This typically happens when the posterior has sharp ridges or funnels: the step size that works in flat regions is too large for the narrow parts, causing numerical errors to explode.

A small number of divergences (say <1% of samples) may be acceptable, but many divergences indicate biased sampling — the sampler is systematically avoiding regions it can’t navigate, so the samples underrepresent those areas.

# Check for divergent transitions. NUTS records one per iteration in the
# `numerical_error` column. One chain is enough to demonstrate the check;
# in practice you would run it over every chain.
n_divergent = sum(skipmissing(vec(chain_good[:numerical_error])))
println("Divergent transitions: $(Int(n_divergent)) / $(niters(chain_good))")
if n_divergent > 0
    println("Consider reparametrising the model or tightening a prior,")
    println("then raising the target acceptance rate, e.g. NUTS(0.95)")
else
    println("No divergent transitions")
end
Divergent transitions: 0 / 2000
No divergent transitions
TipCode explainer
  • chain[:numerical_error] - the per-iteration divergence flag that NUTS records alongside the parameters, 1.0 for a divergent transition and 0.0 otherwise. Summing it counts the divergences.
  • Raising the target acceptance rate makes NUTS take smaller steps, which is usually what a handful of divergences calls for. It is the δ argument: NUTS(0.95) keeps the default warmup length, and NUTS(n_adapts, δ) sets both. It plays the role that adapt_delta does in Stan.

Problem 4: Multi-modal posteriors

Some posteriors have multiple peaks, and a single chain can settle into one and never see the others. The standard responses are:

  • A prior that rules out the implausible mode, where one of them is not credible on knowledge you already hold. The prior has to be defensible on its own terms; one adopted because a mode is inconvenient is rigging the answer.
  • A mixture model, where the modes are genuinely different explanations and the data support both. A single posterior straddling two regimes is the wrong object.
  • Use more advanced samplers (parallel tempering, etc.)

Multimodality is usually a property of the model and the data rather than of the sampler, so the first question is which mode you believe and why, or whether you believe all of them, which is a matter for Model checking.

NoteExample: Detecting multimodality

Here’s an artificial example with two modes to show how multiple chains help:

# Create a artificial multimodal example
@model function multimodal_example()
    x ~ Normal(0, 5)  # Wide prior

    # Likelihood with two modes. Subtracting the larger log-density before
    # exponentiating keeps the mixture stable when both components are tiny.
    mode1_loglik = logpdf(Normal(-2, 0.5), x)
    mode2_loglik = logpdf(Normal(2, 0.5), x)
    largest = max(mode1_loglik, mode2_loglik)
    Turing.@addlogprob! largest +
        log(0.5 * exp(mode1_loglik - largest) + 0.5 * exp(mode2_loglik - largest))
end
multimodal_example (generic function with 2 methods)
TipCode explainer
  • Turing.@addlogprob! manually adds a value to the log-probability of the model. This is useful when you can’t express the likelihood using ~ syntax — here we need a mixture of two Normals, which requires computing the log-probability by hand.
  • The ~ syntax (e.g. x ~ Normal(0, 5)) automatically adds the log-density to the model’s total log-probability. @addlogprob! does the same thing, but you compute the value yourself.
# Seeded so the four chains below reliably split between the two modes, which is
# the behaviour this example is about.
Random.seed!(6)

# Single chain might miss one mode
chain_single = sample(multimodal_example(), NUTS(), 1000)

# Multiple chains more likely to find both modes
chains_multi = [sample(multimodal_example(), NUTS(), 1000) for _ in 1:4]
p = plot(title = "Multimodal Posterior")
for (i, chain) in enumerate(chains_multi)
    density!(p, chain[:x], alpha = 0.7, label = "Chain $i")
end
plot!(p)
# Combine the separate chains into one object so R̂ can compare them
combined = hcat(chains_multi...)
DataFrame(rhat(combined))
1×2 DataFrame
Row param stat
VarName… Float64
1 x 1.89352

Chains that settle in different modes disagree about the mean, and R̂ is the statistic that notices.

The complete workflow

  1. Run multiple chains (at least 4)
  2. Check the trace plots
  3. Calculate R̂ and ESS
  4. Check for divergences (NUTS)
  5. Run a posterior predictive check, which is the next session
  6. Rerun with more samples or different settings if any of these come back badly

Advanced diagnostics

This section covers the details behind the diagnostics above, and two things worth having when one of them fails. If you’re short on time, you can skip ahead to the troubleshooting guide — the core diagnostics (R̂, ESS, trace plots) from Quantitative diagnostics are sufficient for most analyses, though check tail ESS below before quoting a credible interval.

What rhat actually computes

The formula in the R̂ section is the statistic as Gelman and Rubin defined it. Vehtari et al. (2021) wrap three transformations around it, and what rhat() gives you is the result of all three.

Split

Each of the mm chains is cut in half, giving 2m2m half-chains of n/2n/2 draws, and the ordinary formula is applied to those.

Comparing whole chains against each other cannot see a chain that is drifting within itself. Such a chain contributes one mean like any other, and a mean is all the comparison looks at, so a chain that spent its first half in one place and its second half somewhere else is indistinguishable from one that sat still. Splitting turns that drift into a disagreement between its own two halves, which the formula can see.

It is also what lets R̂ mean anything at all when you have only one chain, since the first half is then compared against the second.

rhat_split = DataFrame(rhat(chain_multi))
println("Split-R̂ values (recommended):")
for row in eachrow(rhat_split)
    println("  $(row.param): $(round(row.stat, digits = 4))")
end
Split-R̂ values (recommended):
  R_0: 1.0003
  D_inf: 1.0002

Rank normalise

Pool all SS draws across every chain, rank them with ties averaged to give rir_i, and push the ranks through the normal quantile function:

zi=Φ−1(ri−3/8S+1/4)z_i = \Phi^{-1}\!\left(\frac{r_i - 3/8}{S + 1/4}\right)

The offsets keep the largest and smallest ranks off ±∞\pm\infty: a plain ri/Sr_i/S would send the top rank to Φ−1(1)\Phi^{-1}(1).

WW and BB are then computed on the zz rather than on the draws, and two things follow. R̂ becomes defined even for a posterior with no finite variance, because the zz are normal scores and always have one. And it stops depending on how you parameterise, since ranks see only order, so fitting a rate or its logarithm gives the same answer.

Fold, and take the worst

Everything so far compares where the chains sit, so chains that agree on the centre and disagree on the spread pass it.

Folding replaces each draw by its distance from the pooled median, fi=|xi−median⁡(x)|f_i = \lvert x_i - \operatorname{median}(x) \rvert. A chain with a wider spread than the others then has larger fif_i on average, so a disagreement about spread becomes a disagreement about the mean of ff, which is the thing the formula can already see. The same rank-normalised R̂ is computed on those. What you get back is the larger of the two:

R̂rank=max⁡(R̂bulk,R̂fold)\hat{R}_{\text{rank}} = \max\left(\hat{R}_{\text{bulk}},\ \hat{R}_{\text{fold}}\right)

Either failure is a failure, which is why it is the maximum rather than an average.

In MCMCDiagnosticTools the folded one is kind = :tail, which is not the same thing as the tail ESS in the next section.

Raising the target acceptance rate

δ\delta is the target Metropolis acceptance probability for a NUTS trajectory, and it defaults to 0.65. Warmup tunes the step size ϵ\epsilon to hit it, using the average over the trajectory,

α=min⁡(1,exp(H(θ0,p0)−H(θ,p)))\alpha = \min\left(1,\ \exp\left(H(\theta_0, p_0) - H(\theta, p)\right)\right)

so a δ\delta close to 1 demands that the leapfrog integrator conserve HH almost exactly, which it can only do with a small ϵ\epsilon. That is why raising δ\delta cures divergences, and it costs computation, since a trajectory of the same length then needs more leapfrog steps and so more gradient evaluations.

This is similar to the acceptance rate targeted by random-walk Metropolis, which the MCMC session tunes by hand and then adapts automatically with RAM.

Bulk and tail ESS

Bulk ESS governs how well the centre of the distribution is resolved, so it is the number behind a posterior mean or median. Tail ESS governs the extreme quantiles, so it is the number behind the ends of a credible interval, and it is the one to check before quoting a 95% interval. A chain can have plenty of bulk ESS and still not support the interval you were about to report.

NoteWhat the two are computed on

Bulk ESS is the effective sample size of the rank-normalised draws, using the same zz as the R̂ callout in the previous section:

bulk ESS=ESS(z)\text{bulk ESS} = \text{ESS}(z)

Tail ESS is not an effective sample size of the draws at all. It is the effective sample size of a different quantity: for a quantile qq, the series I(xi<q)I(x_i < q), which is 1 when a draw falls below the quantile and 0 otherwise. That series has its own autocorrelation, and how fast it decorrelates is what determines how well the quantile is pinned down. It is computed for the 5% and 95% quantiles and reports the worse of them:

tail ESS=min⁡(ESS(q0.05),ESS(q0.95))\text{tail ESS} = \min\big(\text{ESS}(q_{0.05}),\ \text{ESS}(q_{0.95})\big)

That min is why tail ESS is often, though not always, the smaller number.

Note the symmetry with R̂. R̂ reports the larger of its bulk and tail, because either failure is a failure. ESS reports the smaller, because either shortage limits what you can report. The word “tail” means different things in the two: folded draws for R̂, extreme quantiles for ESS.

ess_bulk = DataFrame(ess(chain_multi, kind = :bulk))
ess_tail = DataFrame(ess(chain_multi, kind = :tail))

println("Bulk ESS (central posterior):")
for row in eachrow(ess_bulk)
    println("  $(row.param): $(round(row.stat, digits = 0))")
end

println("\nTail ESS (posterior tails):")
for row in eachrow(ess_tail)
    println("  $(row.param): $(round(row.stat, digits = 0))")
end
Bulk ESS (central posterior):
  R_0: 941.0
  D_inf: 976.0

Tail ESS (posterior tails):
  R_0: 890.0
  D_inf: 848.0

The two need not agree, and it is the smaller of them that limits what you can report. They are close here, with the tail slightly ahead. A posterior that the sampler crosses easily in the middle but reaches only occasionally at the edges gives the opposite pattern, and an interval quoted from it is less well determined than the posterior mean printed beside it.

Energy diagnostics (for HMC/NUTS)

NUTS uses Hamiltonian dynamics. Energy plots help diagnose geometric problems:

What to look for: the two histograms below should have similar widths and overlap well. A marginal energy distribution much wider than the spread of energy changes between iterations means the sampler is not travelling far enough through the distribution in each trajectory, which is the geometry problem funnels produce. The formal version of this comparison is the energy Bayesian fraction of missing information (E-BFMI) statistic, and the overlay is its eyeball equivalent.

NoteWhat E-BFMI measures

Each iteration gives the puck a fresh push, and E-BFMI asks whether those pushes are big enough to carry it across the surface rather than around one part of it.

The energy is the Hamiltonian, the negative log posterior at the current parameters plus a kinetic term 12p⊤M−1p\tfrac{1}{2}p^\top M^{-1} p from the momentum, and it is what chain[:hamiltonian_energy] records. Each iteration draws a fresh momentum, and the leapfrog integrator roughly conserves the Hamiltonian within a trajectory, so the change between one iteration and the next comes almost entirely from that refresh. The push is that refresh.

Writing EnE_n for the energy at iteration nn,

E-BFMÎ=∑n=2N(En−En−1)2∑n=1N(En−E‾)2\widehat{\text{E-BFMI}} = \frac{\sum_{n=2}^{N} (E_n - E_{n-1})^2}{\sum_{n=1}^{N} (E_n - \bar{E})^2}

The numerator is how far the sampler moves in energy from one iteration to the next, which is the spread of the energy-change histogram below. The denominator is the spread of energy it has to cover, which is the spread of the marginal energy histogram beside it. A small ratio means the trajectories are not long enough to explore that spread, which is the failure funnels produce, and 0.3 is the threshold usually quoted. Reading the two histograms against each other is the same comparison, drawn rather than divided. See Betancourt (2017).

# Energy diagnostic plot. Like the divergence flag, the Hamiltonian energy is
# recorded as a column, and one chain is enough to show the comparison.
energy = vec(chain_good[:hamiltonian_energy])
energy_changes = diff(energy)
histogram(
    energy .- mean(energy), title = "Energy Distribution", xlabel = "Centred energy",
    ylabel = "Frequency", alpha = 0.5, label = "marginal energy"
)
histogram!(energy_changes .- mean(energy_changes), alpha = 0.5, label = "energy changes")

Troubleshooting guide

Problem Symptoms Solutions
Poor mixing Trace plots show trends, low ESS Look for correlated or non-identified parameters, reparametrise, then NUTS and longer runs
Multimodality High R̂, different chain means A property of the model and data; multiple chains detect it, better initialisation helps
Divergences NUTS warnings, biased sampling Reparametrise, tighten a prior with mass in a pathological region, then raise the target acceptance rate
Slow convergence High autocorrelation, low ESS Check identifiability, reparametrise, then a better algorithm and longer runs
Non-stationarity Trending trace plots Check the model specification, then see Problem 2

Most of what looks like a sampler problem is a model or prior problem, and these diagnostics tell you that something is wrong rather than what. Model checking is where that gets settled.

Practical example: Debugging a problematic model

Let’s create and diagnose a problematic model:

# Poorly specified model with correlations and poor scaling
@model function problematic_model()
    # Poor scaling: one parameter much larger than others
    R_0 ~ Normal(0, 100)     # Wrong scale
    D_inf ~ Normal(0, 0.01)  # Very tight

    # Add some correlation structure to make it harder
    x1 ~ Normal(R_0, 1)
    x2 ~ Normal(R_0, 1)

    # Some fake observations
    for i in 1:10
        0.0 ~ Normal(x1 + x2 - 2*R_0, 0.1)
    end
end
problematic_model (generic function with 2 methods)
# This model will have problems. Sample it twice, once with a single chain and
# once with several, so that the two can be compared below. Seeded so that the
# comparison the text describes is the one on the page.
Random.seed!(2)
chain_problematic_one = sample(problematic_model(), NUTS(), 1000)
chain_problematic = sample(problematic_model(), NUTS(), MCMCThreads(), 1000, n_chains)
# Diagnose it. Each table gets its own cell, because `println` output is
# collected separately from displayed tables and would otherwise arrive
# detached from the label naming it.
println("R̂ from a single chain:")
DataFrame(rhat(chain_problematic_one))

DataFrame(rhat(chain_problematic))

The first table is the single chain and the second is several chains, on the same model with the same number of draws per chain. Only the second is outside the usual 1.1 threshold. The third table shows how little independent information those draws carry. Split-R̂ on one chain compares the first half of a chain against its second half, and a chain that never leaves the region it started in has little to disagree with. Several chains start from different points, and that is what gives R̂ something to detect.

TipExercise: Diagnose and fix the problematic model
  1. Look at the trace plots and quantitative diagnostics above. What specific problems can you identify?
  2. Which parameters show the worst R̂ and ESS values?
  3. Try modifying the problematic_model above to improve its behaviour. Hint: Change the prior scales to be more similar across parameters, or remove the correlation structure.
  4. Run the modified model and compare the diagnostics.
TipSolution

The problems are:

  • Mismatched scales: R_0 ~ Normal(0, 100) is very wide while D_inf ~ Normal(0, 0.01) is extremely tight. The sampler struggles to adapt its step size to work well for both simultaneously.
  • Redundant parameters: x1 and x2 both depend on R_0 and appear only as x1 + x2 - 2*R_0, making them poorly identified — many combinations of x1 and x2 give the same sum.

A fixed version:

@model function fixed_model()
    R_0 ~ Normal(0, 1)       # Moderate scale
    D_inf ~ Normal(0, 1)     # Same scale as R_0

    x1 ~ Normal(R_0, 1)
    x2 ~ Normal(R_0, 1)

    for i in 1:10
        0.0 ~ Normal(x1 + x2 - 2*R_0, 0.1)
    end
end

chain_fixed = sample(fixed_model(), NUTS(), MCMCThreads(), 1000, n_chains)
plot(chain_fixed)
println("R̂ values:")
DataFrame(rhat(chain_fixed))
R̂ values:
4×2 DataFrame
Row param stat
VarName… Float64
1 R_0 0.999684
2 D_inf 1.00131
3 x1 1.00006
4 x2 1.00007 
println("ESS values:")
DataFrame(ess(chain_fixed))
ESS values:
4×2 DataFrame
Row param stat
VarName… Float64
1 R_0 644.088
2 D_inf 1101.99
3 x1 662.967
4 x2 802.283

Both models are now sampled the same way, so the two sets of diagnostics can be read against each other.

ESS is the sharper signal. For three of the four parameters it is two orders of magnitude lower for the problematic model than for the fixed one, from the same number of iterations.

R̂ separates them too. It cannot on its own tell you that a chain is usable, though: it compares chains against each other, and the single-chain R̂ printed earlier passed this very model while its effective sample size stayed in single figures. That is the argument for running several chains and reading more than one number, which is what the workflow above asks for.

The general recipe:

  1. Reparametrise (e.g. centered parameterisations)
  2. Match prior scales across parameters
  3. Extend the warmup period
  4. Check whether the model specification itself is doing something wrong

How the pieces fit together

After three sessions, you now have a complete workflow for Bayesian inference with deterministic models. In Bayesian inference with mathematical models, you learned the core concepts: priors encode beliefs before seeing data, likelihoods measure how well parameters explain observations, and Bayes’ theorem combines them into a posterior. In MCMC, you saw how to sample from posteriors that are too complex for grid search - from basic Metropolis-Hastings through adaptive methods (RAM) to gradient-based samplers (NUTS). This session covered diagnostics: trace plots for visual assessment, R̂ for convergence, and ESS for effective sample size.

The workflow: Define model → Run MCMC → Check convergence → Check model fit → Iterate

Learning points

TipLearning points
  • Always check convergence - never trust MCMC without diagnostics
  • Multiple chains are essential for robust inference
  • R̂ < 1.1 and ESS > 100 are minimum requirements
  • Ideally R̂ < 1.01 and ESS > several hundred.
  • NUTS is usually better than basic Metropolis-Hastings
  • When in doubt, run longer and use more chains
  • Reach for the model before the sampler — most of what looks like a sampler problem is a model or prior problem

MCMC only works if you use it correctly. Diagnostics are not optional.

References

  • Vehtari et al. (2021). Rank-normalization, folding, and localization: An improved R̂ for assessing convergence of MCMC. Bayesian Analysis 16(2), 667-718. (Modern R̂ and ESS)
  • Gelman and Rubin (1992). Inference from iterative simulation using multiple sequences. Statistical Science 7(4), 457-472. (The original R̂)
  • Geyer (1992). Practical Markov chain Monte Carlo. Statistical Science 7(4), 473-483. (The effective sample size estimator and its truncation rule)
  • Gelman et al. (2013). Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed. Chapman & Hall/CRC. (Chapter 11 covers diagnostics)
  • FlexiChains.jl documentation - the chain type this course uses, and its diagnostics
  • ArviZ - Exploratory analysis of Bayesian models (Python, with Julia bindings via ArviZ.jl)
